pos: n. pl. (searchings of heart; inward examinations, self-questionings)
etymology: From search, Old French cerchier, from Latin circare, to go about or round. The Hebrew cheqer means a searching out or investigation, from chaqar, to dig into.
biblical_def: In the roll-call of Deborah's song, Reuben is twice mentioned and twice found wanting: “Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart” (Judges 5:16). Searchings of heart are inward examinations, deep self-questionings. The verse before had used a kindred phrase: “For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart” (Judges 5:15). Reuben debated. The tribe held councils, weighed the matter, examined motives, and did not come. Deborah sets that against Zebulun and Naphtali, who jeoparded their lives unto the death. The searchings were real and may well have been sincere; they were also, in the event, a substitute for obedience. Scripture elsewhere commends the searching of the heart in the strongest terms — “Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23) — but notice who does the searching there. Self-examination offered to God issues in action; self-examination held among the sheepfolds issues in deliberation that never ends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SEARCHING, a looking into; inquiry; examination; SEARCH, to look over or through for the purpose of finding.
webster_full: SEARCHING, ppr. Looking into or over; exploring; examining.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something.
To inquire; to seek for; to examine; as, to search the heart.
Hebrew cheqer, a searching out, from chaqar, to dig into.

Jdg 5:15

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
corruption_summary: Endless introspection takes the place of obedience, and the examining of motives becomes the respectable reason for never acting.
corruption_paragraphs: Deborah's line about Reuben is one of the quietest rebukes in Scripture and one of the most searching. The tribe did not refuse in defiance; it deliberated. Great searchings of heart, and no men at Kishon. A therapeutic age multiplies exactly this failure, teaching believers to process their feelings about a duty rather than to do it, and dignifying the delay as discernment.

Self-examination is commanded: examine yourselves whether ye be in the faith, and let a man examine himself before eating of that bread. But the Psalmist's pattern turns the work outward and upward, asking God to search him, and ending in a prayer to be led in the way everlasting. Searching that ends in the self ends nowhere. The test of true searching of heart is whether a man goes down to the battle when the LORD's call comes.

pos: n. pl. (light sleeps; drowsings upon the bed)
etymology: From slumber, Middle English slumeren, from Old English sluma, light sleep. The Hebrew tenumah means slumber or drowsiness, distinguished from deep sleep.
biblical_def: Elihu answers Job's complaint that God does not speak by listing the ways He does: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed” (Job 33:15). Slumberings are light sleeps, the drowsing state at the edge of unconsciousness, and the whole verse insists that God addresses men where they are least in control of themselves. Elihu's premise is stated first: “For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not” (Job 33:14). The fault is not in God's silence but in man's dullness. And the stated purpose of the night-speaking is instruction and rescue: “Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction” (Job 33:16), that He may withdraw man from his purpose and hide pride from him. The dictionary notes carefully what this does and does not establish. In the patriarchal age, before the canon was complete, God did speak by dreams and visions, and Scripture records it without apology. With the canon closed, the Spirit speaks in and by the written Word, and no slumbering now brings revelation.

webster_full: SLUMBER, v.i. To sleep lightly; to doze; to be in the state between sleeping and waking.
SLUMBER, n. Light sleep; sleep not deep or sound.
SLUMBERING, ppr. Dozing; sleeping lightly.
Hebrew tenumah, slumber or drowsiness, as distinct from deep sleep.

corruption_summary: Dreams are treated as a live channel of fresh revelation for the church today, which sets private impressions beside the completed Scriptures.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic and prophetic movements cite Job 33:15 and Joel 2 to establish dreams and night visions as a continuing means by which God delivers new messages, and the practical result is a stream of personal revelations that nobody can test and that routinely contradict one another. The dictionary holds the sufficiency of Scripture: the canon is closed, and what God has to say to His church He has said in the Book.

The opposite error is to deny that God ever spoke so, or to be embarrassed by the patriarchal narratives. Scripture reports them as fact. Joseph, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Joseph the husband of Mary and Paul at Troas all received genuine communications in the night, and Hebrews marks the change of administration precisely: God who spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. Elihu's point survives the change of means intact: God speaks, and man's problem is that he perceiveth it not.

pos: n. (a pause, a ceasing for a time; a break in continuity)
etymology: From Latin intermittere, to leave off in the middle, from inter (between) and mittere (to send or let go). The Hebrew phrase in Lamentations is min hugoth, without ceasing or respite.
biblical_def: Jeremiah's weeping over fallen Jerusalem is described in a clause that will not let itself end: “Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission” (Lamentations 3:49). An intermission is a pause, a leaving-off in the middle, and the prophet denies himself even that. The next line gives the terminus he is waiting for: “Till the LORD look down, and behold from heaven” (Lamentations 3:50). This is not grief without purpose; it is intercession that refuses to stop until God acts. And the same chapter holds the most famous confession of hope in the Old Testament, set in the middle of the lament: “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not” (Lamentations 3:22). The two belong together. Jeremiah is not choosing between grief and hope but holding both without intermission, weeping over a judgment he had foretold and could not avert, and resting on mercies that are new every morning. This is the godly pattern for a man who loves a people under chastening.

webster_full: INTERMISSION, n. Cessation for a time; pause; intermediate stop.

corruption_summary: Sustained grief is pathologised as a condition to be resolved on a timetable, and the lament, which Scripture gives a whole book to, is treated as a stage to pass through.
corruption_paragraphs: Grief in modern handling is a process with phases and an expected terminus; prolonged weeping is read as a disorder. Scripture is not careless about the sufferer, and it does not romanticise misery; but it gives a book of the Bible to lament and sets one of its great statements of hope inside the longest lament in the canon. Jeremiah's eye runs down without intermission, and he is not sick.

What orders his grief is its object and its terminus. He weeps for the daughter of his people, and he weeps till the LORD look down. That is intercession rather than despair, and it is the pattern for every believer who loves a church, a family or a nation under judgment: tears that do not stop, laid before a God whose compassions fail not. The therapeutic framework has no category for such weeping, which is why it must call it a condition.

pos: n. pl. (stabbings; thrusts such as a sword makes)
etymology: From pierce, Old French percer, perhaps from Latin pertundere, to thrust through. The Hebrew madqeroth means thrusts or stabs, from daqar, to pierce through.
biblical_def: Proverbs sets two tongues side by side: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health” (Proverbs 12:18). Piercings are stabbings, the thrusts a blade makes, and the proverb is describing a manner of speech rather than a single cruel sentence — a habit of talk that punctures. The contrast is medical: the wise tongue is health, literally healing. So speech is never neutral in Proverbs; every tongue is either a weapon or a medicine. The same book gives the scale of the matter: “A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4). A breach in the spirit is a wound inside a person, where no bandage reaches. James takes up the theme at length and calls the tongue a fire. The dictionary notes that faithful words sometimes do wound — faithful are the wounds of a friend, and a rebuke is commanded — but the difference is in the aim. A sword thrust intends damage; a surgeon's cut intends health.

webster_full: PIERCING, ppr. Penetrating; entering, as a pointed instrument.

corruption_summary: Wounding speech is excused as candour or zeal for truth, while the correction Scripture commands is avoided for fear of causing offence.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures run in opposite directions and both cite Scripture. The first calls its piercings honesty: hard words are defended as plain speaking, and the damage is laid at the hearer's door for being thin-skinned. Proverbs answers it directly, naming such a tongue a sword and the wise tongue health. Zeal that leaves a breach in the spirit is not zeal for truth.

The second failure never speaks at all. Rebuke is withheld, sin left unnamed, and the silence called kindness; yet Scripture says faithful are the wounds of a friend, and that he who rebukes shall be loved more in the end than he who flatters. The difference between the sword and the scalpel is not the sharpness but the aim. Paul's rule governs both: speech alway with grace, seasoned with salt, knowing how we ought to answer every man.

pos: n. pl. (loud cries of acclamation; shouts of triumph or praise)
etymology: From shout, of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Old Norse skuta, to taunt. The Hebrew teshuah means a shout or acclamation, from a root meaning to cry out.
biblical_def: Zechariah's fourth vision answers the discouragement of a small rebuilding: “Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it” (Zechariah 4:7). Shoutings are loud acclamations, and the word placed in their mouths is remarkable: not well done, not at last, but Grace, grace unto it. The finished work is credited wholly to God's favour. The preceding verse supplies the principle the whole vision exists to teach: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). Ezra records what such shoutings sounded like when the foundation was laid: “And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid” (Ezra 3:11) — though the same chapter notes that the old men who had seen the first house wept. The great mountain of opposition becomes a plain, and the shout that goes up over the last stone is a shout about grace.

webster_full: SHOUTING, n. The act of shouting; a loud outcry expressive of joy or triumph.

corruption_summary: Zechariah 4:6 is detached from its context and used as a slogan against ordinary diligence, when the vision commissions a man to finish a building God would finish through him.
corruption_paragraphs: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” is among the most quoted and least contextualised verses in Scripture. Pulled out of Zechariah 4 it becomes a general spiritualism, sometimes used to excuse the neglect of planning, labour and competence, as though effort were the opposite of the Spirit.

The vision says the opposite. The man addressed is a governor in the middle of a construction project; the Spirit's work is that Zerubbabel's own hands shall finish it, and the next verses rebuke those who despise the day of small things. What is denied is not diligence but self-reliance, the might and power of man as the source of the outcome. That is why the shout over the headstone is Grace, grace unto it: a finished work, done by real hands, and credited entirely to God.

pos: n. pl. (the spreading out of a thing; here, the expanse of storm clouds)
etymology: From spread, Old English spraedan, to stretch out. The Hebrew miphras means an expanse or spreading, from paras, to spread abroad.
biblical_def: Elihu's long meditation on the weather turns into a question no man can answer: “Also can any understand the spreadings of the clouds, or the noise of his tabernacle?” (Job 36:29). Spreadings are the spreading out of the storm, the vast canopy that unrolls across a sky before the thunder; and his tabernacle is the cloud-pavilion God dwells behind. Elihu is not asking a meteorological question but a theological one, and he has already given the conclusion: “Behold, God is great, and we know him not, neither can the number of his years be searched out” (Job 36:26). Two chapters later the LORD Himself takes up the same method, answering Job out of the whirlwind with question after question about things Job cannot do or explain. Elihu anticipates it: “God thundereth marvellously with his voice; great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend” (Job 37:5). The doctrine is the incomprehensibility of God. He is truly known as He reveals Himself and never exhaustively known, and the honest end of looking at a sky is worship rather than mastery.

webster_full: SPREADING, ppr. Extending; expanding; dilating.

corruption_summary: The incomprehensibility of God is pressed into agnosticism, as though a God not exhaustively known could not be truly known at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Elihu's unanswerable questions are regularly enlisted on behalf of a theological agnosticism: since no one understands the spreadings of the clouds, no one can speak with confidence about God, and doctrinal definition is presumption. The move is popular wherever confessional clarity is unwelcome, and it misuses a real attribute.

The dictionary holds both halves of the classical doctrine. God is incomprehensible: not one of His attributes can be exhausted by a creature, and divine simplicity means He is not assembled out of parts we can inventory. And God is truly known: He has revealed Himself in His works and decisively in His Word and His Son, so that what He has said may be confessed without hesitation. Job is not told that God is unknowable. He is answered out of the whirlwind by the God who then calls him friend and restores him. Mystery at the edges is the reason for worship, never a warrant for vagueness at the centre.

pos: v. (wrapping within itself; enfolding, turning in upon itself)
etymology: From in and fold, Old English fealdan: to wrap within. The Hebrew mithlaqqachath is a reflexive participle meaning taking hold of itself, used of fire that catches on itself.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's opening vision begins with weather and ends in glory: “And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” (Ezekiel 1:4). A fire infolding itself is a fire wrapping and catching on itself, flame turning continually inward and feeding on its own blaze; the Hebrew participle is reflexive and exact. The image is of a self-sustaining fire, which is precisely what no earthly fire is: every flame man has seen consumes something outside itself and dies when the fuel is gone. Moses had seen the same impossibility in a bush that burned and was not consumed. The vision closes by naming what it was: “This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face” (Ezekiel 1:28). Hebrews states the doctrine in four words: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). The self-infolding flame is the aseity of God made visible to a prophet by a river in Babylon.

webster_full: INFOLD, v.t. To involve; to wrap up or inwrap; to inclose.

For our God is a consuming fire.
corruption_summary: The self-existence of God is traded for a deity who needs the world — who grows, is changed by it, and depends on it to be fully Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Process theology makes God and the world mutually dependent, so that God becomes with His creation and is enriched by it; open theism denies exhaustive foreknowledge and makes the future genuinely open to Him as well as to us. Both deny what the self-infolding fire pictures: a God who burns without fuel. The dictionary holds the classical attributes — aseity, immutability, impassibility, divine simplicity in the Reformed scholastic sense — and names these systems as departures from theology proper and from every historic Christian confession.

The pastoral weight is immediate. A God who needs the world cannot be trusted with it, since His own completion is at stake in the outcome. The God of Ezekiel 1 is a fire that feeds on itself, utterly independent of every creature, and it is from the midst of that fire that a voice speaks and commissions a prophet to a rebellious house. He does not need Ezekiel. That is exactly why the commission is grace.

pos: adv. (alone; in solitude, apart from others)
etymology: From solitary, Latin solitarius, alone, from solus, alone, with the adverbial -ly. The Hebrew badad means to be separate or alone.
biblical_def: Micah's closing prayer asks for a particular kind of pasturing: “Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old” (Micah 7:14). To dwell solitarily is to dwell alone, and the word carries both of the senses Scripture gives to Israel's separateness. It is her security, for Balaam prophesied that she should dwell alone and not be reckoned among the nations, and that separateness was covenant privilege. It is also her present loneliness, a remnant in the wood while Bashan and Gilead lie in other hands. Micah asks the Shepherd to feed such a flock, and the prophecy ends in the great doxology: “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?” (Micah 7:18). And God's habit with the solitary is stated plainly elsewhere: “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6). The believer's separation from the world is permanent; his isolation is not, for God gathers those who dwell alone into a household.

corruption_summary: Solitary religion is accepted as a normal Christian condition, so that separation from the world is confused with separation from the church.
corruption_paragraphs: A spirituality without the local church is now common and often sincere: the believer keeps his faith, drops the congregation, and calls the result a personal walk. Wounds from real failures in real churches have driven much of it. But Micah's flock dwelling solitarily in the wood is a picture of loss, not of health, and the prophet prays for it to be fed and gathered.

Scripture distinguishes two things the modern usage confuses. Separation from the world is commanded and permanent: be ye separate, saith the Lord. Isolation from the people of God is a condition to be remedied, and God Himself remedies it, for He setteth the solitary in families. The dictionary holds the local church with its two offices and plurality of elders as the ordinary place of Christian life, where the ordinances are administered and the solitary are set in a household.

pos: n. (a standing place; an appointed post or office)
etymology: From Latin statio, a standing or post, from stare, to stand. A station is the place where one is set to stand. The Hebrew maamad means a standing place or office, from amad, to stand.
biblical_def: Isaiah is sent to Shebna, the treasurer over the house, with a sentence of removal: “And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down” (Isaiah 22:19). A station is an appointed post, the place where a man is set to stand. Shebna had carved himself a sepulchre on high and behaved as though the office were his property; God calls it a station, which is to say a stewardship, and removes him from it. A successor is named in the next verse: “And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah” (Isaiah 22:20). And of Eliakim is said a thing that reaches past Eliakim: “And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isaiah 22:22). The risen Christ claims that very language in Revelation 3, calling Himself He that hath the key of David. Every office in church, state and household is a station, held at the pleasure of the One who holds the key.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STATION, the spot or place where a person or thing stands; situation; rank; office; employment.
webster_full: STATION, n. The spot or place where a person or thing stands.
A post assigned; office; the part or department of public duty which a person undertakes.
Situation; position; rank; condition of life.
From Latin statio, a standing or post, from stare, to stand.
Isaiah 22:19 says, I will drive thee from thy station.
scriptures: And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah:
And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
corruption_summary: Office is treated as personal property or personal identity, so that the holder cannot distinguish the removal of a post from the destruction of himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Shebna built his own tomb on a height while serving in another man's house, and the detail tells the whole story: he had stopped thinking of the office as a station and begun thinking of it as an estate. The pattern is thoroughly modern. A pastorate, a board seat, a platform or a title becomes the man, and the suggestion that he might be moved from it is heard as an attack on his person.

Scripture's word station refuses that. A post is somewhere one is set to stand, by someone else, for a time; God gives it, God removes from it, and He names the successor in the next breath. The doctrine is sharpened by the fact that Eliakim's commission is quoted by the risen Christ of Himself. He holds the key; every other officeholder holds a station. A man who knows the difference can be removed without being destroyed.
roots_summary: Latin statio, a post, from stare, to stand; Hebrew maamad, a standing place; Isaiah 22:19 drives Shebna from his station.
roots_lines: Latin statio, a standing or post, from stare, to stand.
Hebrew maamad, a standing place or office, from amad, to stand.
Isaiah 22:19 is the only occurrence of station in the Authorized Version.
Shebna had hewn himself a sepulchre on high while serving in another's house.
Isaiah 22:22 is claimed by the risen Christ in Revelation 3.
usage: I will drive thee from thy station
names an office as an appointed post, not a possession
held under the One who has the key of the house of David

pos: v. (to cease, to leave off; here, to be severed from a possession)
etymology: From Old French discontinuer, from Latin dis- (apart) and continuare, to continue. In older legal English, to discontinue an estate is to break the continuity of a title. The Hebrew shamat means to let drop or release.
biblical_def: Jeremiah announces the loss of the inheritance in a word drawn from the law of tenure: “And thou, even thyself, shalt discontinue from thine heritage that I gave thee; and I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in the land which thou knowest not: for ye have kindled a fire in mine anger, which shall burn for ever” (Jeremiah 17:4). To discontinue from a heritage is to be severed from it, to have the continuity of possession broken. The Hebrew is the verb used for the release of land in the sabbatical year, which gives the sentence a terrible irony: Israel would not let the land rest as God commanded, so the land would rest from Israel. And the chapter states the root sin and its opposite in two of the most famous verses in the prophets: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD” (Jeremiah 17:5), and “Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is” (Jeremiah 17:7). An inheritance can be discontinued. The hope of the man who trusts in the LORD cannot.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DISCONTINUE, to leave off; to cease from; to break off; in law, to lose or break the continuity of an estate.
webster_full: DISCONTINUE, v.t. To leave off; to cause to cease; to stop.
To break off; to interrupt.
In law, to lose or break the continuance or continuity of; as, to discontinue an estate.
Hebrew shamat, to let drop or release, as land in the sabbatical year.
Jeremiah 17:4 says, thou shalt discontinue from thine heritage that I gave thee.
scriptures: Jer 17:4

And thou, even thyself, shalt discontinue from thine heritage that I gave thee; and I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in the land which thou knowest not: for ye have kindled a fire in mine anger, which shall burn for ever.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Jer 17:7
Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.
corruption_summary: The warnings of covenant forfeiture are set against the assurance of the elect, so that either the warnings are emptied or assurance is denied.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 17:4 is a hard word, and two systems mishandle it in opposite directions. One treats such passages as proof that a believer may be finally lost, making perseverance a matter of human maintenance. The other, in reaction, so flattens the warnings that no threat in Scripture can be addressed to anyone who has professed faith — the bare once-saved-always-saved reflex that the dictionary distinguishes from the confessional doctrine.

The Reformed position holds both. Perseverance of the saints is the genuine fruit of regeneration, guaranteed by the Father's election, the Son's intercession and the Spirit's indwelling; and the warnings are real means by which God preserves His people, as well as real sentences executed on the merely covenantal and unregenerate — which Judah in Jeremiah's day largely was. The chapter itself puts the two side by side: cursed is the man who makes flesh his arm; blessed is the man whose hope the LORD is. An estate may be discontinued. The One who is Himself the inheritance cannot be.
roots_summary: Latin dis- plus continuare; Hebrew shamat, to release; Jeremiah 17:4 severs Judah from the heritage God gave her.
roots_lines: Latin dis-, apart, and continuare, to continue: to break continuity.

Hebrew shamat, to let drop or release, as land in the sabbatical year.
Jeremiah 17:4 is the only occurrence of discontinue in the Authorized Version.
